summary: Describes how to use the Generic Routing Encapsulation header for network virtualization in multi-tenant data centers. It decouples virtual networks from the physical network so tenants are isolated. It also introduces a network virtualization framework to illustrate use cases.

plainLanguage.summary: Many families can share one apartment building and each feels like they have a private house. This wraps their network traffic so it stays separate.

questions: how does gre provide network virtualization in data centers
how does nvgre use gre key field
subtitle: Tunnelling Ethernet frames in GRE so each tenant in a data center gets its own virtual Layer 2 network.

tldr.problem: Data center VLANs top out at about 4,000 subnets, tie workloads to physical location, and need error-prone reconfiguration when virtual machines move.
tldr.mechanism: NVGRE wraps each tenant Ethernet frame in a GRE header over IP, using the 32-bit GRE Key field to carry a 24-bit Virtual Subnet ID plus an 8-bit FlowID.
tldr.outcome: A 24-bit VSID supports up to 16 million virtual subnets, and virtual machines can be placed anywhere without reconfiguring the physical network.

today: RFC 7637 is an Informational RFC published in September 2015. According to the unit metadata it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Virtualize the Network
sections.content:
Conventional data center designs suit largely static workloads and fragment network and server capacity. Layer 2 networks use the Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol, which blocks redundant paths and wastes capacity. VLANs isolate tenants, but the current VLAN limits theoretically allow for 4,000 subnets, which is no longer enough in a shared infrastructure. Moving workloads by stretching VLANs requires network reconfiguration that is typically error prone.

The RFC lists four design objectives: location-independent addressing, scaling the number of logical Layer 2 and Layer 3 networks regardless of physical topology, preserving Layer 2 semantics as services move, and broadcast isolation without burdening the control plane.

Network virtualization decouples a virtual network from the physical one by virtualizing addresses. Customers can bring their own address spaces, and administrators can place their virtual machines anywhere without reconfiguring switches or routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Old apartment-style numbering ran out of room and made moving house a hassle. NVGRE gives every family a private street that follows them wherever they move.

sections.title: The NVGRE Idea and Its Endpoints
sections.content:
NVGRE creates virtual Layer 2 topologies on top of a physical Layer 3 network by tunnelling Ethernet frames in GRE over IP. Every virtual Layer 2 network has a 24-bit Virtual Subnet Identifier (VSID). A 24-bit VSID supports up to 16 million virtual subnets in one management domain, versus about 4,000 with VLANs. Each VSID is a virtual broadcast domain, and administrators can configure routes between a tenant's virtual subnets.

An NVGRE endpoint is a Network Virtualization Edge (NVE), the ingress and egress point between virtual and physical networks. It can be any physical server or network device, commonly part of a hypervisor. It encapsulates and decapsulates Ethernet frames, ensures Layer 2 semantics and applies isolation policy per VSID. The RFC assumes the destination location information is available to the endpoint, whether from a management plane, control-plane distribution or data-plane learning.

Two address types matter: the Customer Address (CA), the only address that VMs see, and the Provider Address (PA) used in the physical network.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper at the edge of each building puts letters into the bigger envelope when they leave and takes them out again on arrival.

sections.title: The NVGRE Frame Format
sections.content:
NVGRE uses the GRE header of RFC 2784 and the Key extension of RFC 2890. The outer Ethernet header carries the endpoint's MAC address as source and the MAC of the next-hop IP address as destination, with an optional outer VLAN tag. The outer IP header may be IPv4 or IPv6, and its addresses are the PAs. The inner frame carries the tenant's own addresses, the CAs.

In the GRE header the C (Checksum Present) and S (Sequence Number Present) bits MUST be zero, and the K (Key Present) bit MUST be one. The 32-bit Key holds the 24-bit VSID and an 8-bit FlowID that adds per-flow entropy within a VSID. Transit devices MUST NOT modify the FlowID, the encapsulating NVE SHOULD provide as much entropy as possible, and if none is generated it MUST be all zeros. The Protocol Type is 0x6558 (Transparent Ethernet Bridging).

The inner Ethernet frame can be any Ethernet frame, not only IP, and its Frame Check Sequence is not encapsulated. The inner header MUST NOT contain an IEEE 802.1Q tag: the encapsulating NVE MUST remove any existing tag and a decapsulating NVE MUST drop a frame that has one. VSIDs 0 to 0xFFF are reserved for future use, and 0xFFFFFF is reserved for vendor-specific NVE-to-NVE communication.
sections.plainLanguage: The big envelope has a family number written on it and a rule that the inside letter must not carry its own old sorting stickers.

sections.title: Traffic Handling
sections.content:
For unicast, the endpoint encapsulates the Layer 2 packet in GRE using its source PA and the destination PA where the target endpoint lives. The physical network bridges and routes it normally, needing only bidirectional IP connectivity, and the destination endpoint decapsulates it. Policy controls which PA is used when an endpoint has more than one.

For broadcast and multicast inside a virtual subnet, one or more administratively scoped multicast addresses can be assigned to the VSID, with all such traffic encapsulated and sent to that address. Alternatively an NVE can use N-way unicast, sending one encapsulated packet to every NVE in the virtual subnet, which removes the need for multicast in the physical network.

Address acquisition is out of scope. CA and PA space can each be IPv4 or IPv6, and the families do not have to match. Because location information can be preconfigured in an endpoint, broadcast ARP traffic can be proxied locally.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal mail goes straight to one address. Messages for everyone are either sent to a special group mailbox or copied and delivered to each person.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
ECMP: if Equal-Cost Multipath is used, it is RECOMMENDED that the hash use either the outer IP fields and the entire 32-bit Key, or the inner IP and transport fields. Fragmentation: a sender NVE MUST NOT fragment NVGRE packets, a receiver MAY discard fragmented ones, and the physical network MTU is RECOMMENDED to accommodate the larger encapsulated frames.

Cross-premise and Internet access: an enterprise can extend its subnets into a public cloud, and a per-tenant VPN gateway running as a VM carries traffic back over a site-to-site tunnel. Internet connectivity needs a gateway that translates between the virtualized CA space and public addresses, such as a load balancer or NAT.

Devices and hosts: routing in the physical network works without changes, but devices doing specialized processing need to parse GRE to see tenant information. Host features such as checksum offload and IPsec SA offload should become NVGRE aware, and the endpoint SHOULD intercept offload requests and translate addresses. Scenarios needing lossless Ethernet may not suit NVGRE. Management and control planes are out of scope. An endpoint can use one PA for many CAs, reducing MAC address table sizes at Top-of-Rack switches.
sections.plainLanguage: The big envelopes must not be cut in pieces, so the roads need to be wide enough. Special gates are needed to send mail out of the building to the wider world.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Extending a Layer 2 subnet across the data center increases the scope for spoofing attacks. The RFC suggests mitigation with authentication or encryption such as IPsec or another IP-based mechanism, securing the policy-distribution control plane with existing security protocols, and isolating management traffic in a separate subnet or VLAN.

The GRE checksum is not supported, so the RFC advises deploying NVGRE in a network that provides error detection along the path, for example Ethernet CRC or IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the private streets now stretch across the whole building, someone could pretend to be a neighbor, so locks on the doors and a check that mail was not damaged are important.
